note: Curated waypoint descriptions, keyed by the stable ids in data/waypoint-ids.json. Applied by scripts/build-trails.ts (overriding any description from the GPX/GeoJSON source) and uploadable to the comments API with scripts/upload-descriptions.ts. Listed east to west, from the Alice Springs Telegraph Station to Redbank Gorge, matching the km order of the generated trail data, with the off-route and alternate-route waypoints appended at the end in the same east-to-west order.

descriptions.name: Alice Springs Telegraph Station
descriptions.description: Water tank at the trail's eastern trailhead, beside the reserve's day-use area and toilets. Being on the edge of town it is the simplest place to start with full bottles, though the tank is filled by vehicle like every other one on the trail.

descriptions.name: Telegraph Station Trailhead
descriptions.description: The eastern end of the Larapinta Trail, at the historic Alice Springs Telegraph Station reserve on the edge of town. Section 1 starts here, and it is the easiest trailhead of all to reach — most walkers begin or finish with a short lift from Alice Springs.

descriptions.name: Wallaby Gap
descriptions.description: Tank and small camp at a gap in the low hills west of Alice Springs, the usual first night for walkers who start in the afternoon. The tank is refilled by vehicle rather than fed by a spring, so top up here but do not count on finding it full.

descriptions.name: Simpons Gap Trailhead
descriptions.description: Section 1 ends and Section 2 begins at the Simpsons Gap trailhead, reached by road from Alice Springs along Larapinta Drive. The easy access and day-visitor facilities make it a practical place for a food drop or a lift out.

descriptions.name: Simpsons Gap
descriptions.description: Walkers' camp near the Simpsons Gap trailhead, with tent sites and toilets close by. Drinking water comes from a carted tank, so treat what you take and check the level before you plan the next day around it.

descriptions.name: Simpsons Gap
descriptions.description: Simpsons Gap itself is a narrow cleft in the range with a waterhole that often holds through the dry, and black-footed rock-wallabies on the scree at dawn and dusk. The gap is a significant place for Arrernte people — stay on the formed tracks and respect the signage.

descriptions.name: Mulga Camp
descriptions.description: Tank and camp in mulga scrub midway through the long Section 2 walk. Shade is thin around the tank in the middle of the day, and the water is carted in, so plan for it to be low at the end of a dry stretch.

descriptions.name: Jay Creek
descriptions.description: Tank and camp at Jay Creek, at the western end of Section 2. The creek itself only runs after rain and the tank depends on the next vehicle visit, so leave here with enough to reach Standley Chasm.

descriptions.name: Jay Creek Trailhead
descriptions.description: The boundary between Sections 2 and 3, with vehicle access that makes it usable for food drops and shuttles. Some country around Jay Creek is significant to Traditional Owners and the trail is routed to avoid restricted areas — stay on the marked track and follow the signs.

descriptions.name: Millers Flat
descriptions.description: Creekside camp among river gums in the foothills below the Chewings Range on Section 3. An alternative high route branches near here for walkers who would rather take the ridgeline than the valley floor; there is no dependable water at the flat.

descriptions.name: Kiosk: Standley Chasm
descriptions.description: Kiosk at the Standley Chasm visitor area, selling meals, coffee and cold drinks when it is open. Hours are seasonal and it is not a shop for restocking a food bag, but it is the first cooked meal most walkers get after leaving Alice Springs.

descriptions.name: R: Standley Chasm
descriptions.description: One of the standard food-drop points on the trail. Boxes are arranged in advance and brought in by vehicle, so pack yours to survive heat and ants and confirm the arrangement before you start walking.

descriptions.name: Standley Chasm
descriptions.description: Campground at Standley Chasm, run alongside the visitor area and the most comfortable stop on the eastern half of the trail. It sits on Aboriginal-owned land, so check in and follow the operators' directions on where to camp.

descriptions.name: Standley Chasm Trailhead
descriptions.description: Section 3 ends and Section 4 begins here, at the end of the road in from Larapinta Drive. The chasm — a narrow red-walled cleft best seen near midday — is an Aboriginal-owned visitor site, so call in at the front counter before walking up it.

descriptions.name: Brinkley Bluff
descriptions.description: Exposed camp on the crest of the Chewings Range, one of the high points of the whole trail and known for its sunsets and sunrises. There is no water and nothing to break the wind, so carry everything up and think twice if weather is coming in.

descriptions.name: Stuart's Pass
descriptions.description: Camp in the pass below the Brinkley Bluff descent, low enough to escape the worst of the ridge wind. It is a bush site with no facilities and nothing to drink, so arrive carrying the night's water.

descriptions.name: 4/5 Junction
descriptions.description: Camp at the junction where Section 4 ends and Section 5 begins, in the Birthday Waterhole area. A side track leads out to the Birthday Waterhole trailhead, a road-access point used for drops and pickups; the waterhole is seasonal and not something to plan around.

descriptions.name: Fringe Lily Creek
descriptions.description: Small camp in a creek gully on Section 5, named for the fringe lilies that flower here after rain. Any water in the creek is seasonal, so treat finding some as a bonus rather than part of the plan.

descriptions.name: Hugh Gorge Junction
descriptions.description: Camp where the trail meets Hugh Gorge, at the top of the walk down through it. The gorge is rock-hopping country with pools that sometimes have to be waded, so it is worth starting into it fresh in the morning rather than late in the day.

descriptions.name: Hugh Gorge Trailhead
descriptions.description: The boundary between Sections 5 and 6, at the mouth of Hugh Gorge. Vehicle access is by a rough track rather than a sealed road, so it sees far fewer visitors than the trailheads further west.

descriptions.name: Hugh Gorge
descriptions.description: Tank at the Hugh Gorge trailhead camp, the fill point before Section 6 — the longest stretch between trailheads on the trail. The water is carted in, so check the level and take everything you can carry.

descriptions.name: Ghost Gum Flat
descriptions.description: Open camp among ghost gums on the long Section 6 walk, a useful first night out from Hugh Gorge. Shade is patchy through the middle of the day and there is nothing dependable to drink here.

descriptions.name: Rocky Gully
descriptions.description: Camp in a stony gully partway along Section 6, the longest section on the trail. Water is a matter of carted tanks and seasonal pools, so leave Hugh Gorge or Ellery Creek carrying enough for the whole stretch.

descriptions.name: Ellery Creek North
descriptions.description: Walkers' camp on the northern side of Ellery Creek, near Ellery Creek Big Hole. The Big Hole holds water year round and is a famous swim, but it is genuinely cold and deep — people get into trouble swimming it alone.

descriptions.name: Ellery Creek Trailhead
descriptions.description: Section 6 ends and Section 7 begins at Ellery Creek, a busy day-visitor site with a car park and toilets reached from Namatjira Drive. The road access makes it one of the easier places to meet a shuttle or collect a food drop.

descriptions.name: R: Ellery Creek
descriptions.description: Food-drop point at the Ellery Creek trailhead. Boxes are delivered by vehicle and held until you arrive, so arrange the drop before you start and pack it for heat, ants and a long wait.

descriptions.name: Ellery Creek South
descriptions.description: The second of the two walkers' camps at Ellery Creek, on the southern side of the crossing. Facilities are basic and the tank is refilled by vehicle, so treat what you collect and fill before heading into Section 7.

descriptions.name: Serpentine Gorge
descriptions.description: Camp at the end of Section 7, near the mouth of Serpentine Gorge and below the ridge the trail climbs heading west. A steep lookout track above the gorge is the usual evening walk from here.

descriptions.name: R: Serpentine Gorge
descriptions.description: Food-drop point at the Serpentine Gorge trailhead, the last one before the remote country of Sections 8 and 9. Drops come in by vehicle and have to be arranged before you set out.

descriptions.name: Serpentine Gorge Trailhead
descriptions.description: The boundary between Sections 7 and 8, with car-park access off Namatjira Drive and a walk in to the gorge mouth. The waterhole there is significant to Traditional Owners — read the signs at the entrance and respect any request to stay out of the water.

descriptions.name: Serpentine Gorge, Larapinta Trail campsite
descriptions.description: The tank at the Serpentine Gorge walkers' camp, beside the trailhead. It is topped up by vehicle and can run low late in the season, so treat what you take and fill everything before starting Section 8.

descriptions.name: Serpentine Chalet Dam
descriptions.description: Bush camp beside the small dam built to supply the old chalet. It holds water after rain and can be dry otherwise, so treat it as a maybe and carry what you need for the climb into Section 9.

descriptions.name: Serpentine Chalet Dam Trailhead
descriptions.description: Section 8 ends and Section 9 begins at Serpentine Chalet Dam, reached only by a rough four-wheel-drive track off Namatjira Drive. The ruins of the Serpentine Chalet, a short-lived mid-century tourist camp, lie nearby.

descriptions.name: Waterfall Gorge
descriptions.description: Sheltered camp in the gorge on Section 9, in the broken country between the Chewings ridgeline and Ormiston. Water here depends entirely on recent rain — the name describes the shape of the place, not a supply.

descriptions.name: Mt Giles Lookout
descriptions.description: High, open camp looking across to Mt Giles, one of the best places on the trail to watch the light change on the ranges at dawn. There is no water and no shade, so carry everything up; winter nights here are cold and windy.

descriptions.name: Kiosk: Ormiston Gorge
descriptions.description: Kiosk at the Ormiston Gorge visitor area with meals, coffee, cold drinks and a few basics. Opening hours are seasonal and shorter in the hot months, so treat a meal here as a bonus rather than part of the food plan.

descriptions.name: Ormiston Gorge
descriptions.description: Campground at Ormiston Gorge, the most developed stop on the western half of the trail, with toilets and usually hot showers. It is shared with car-based visitors, so expect company through the cooler walking months.

descriptions.name: Ormiston Gorge Trailhead
descriptions.description: Section 9 ends and Section 10 begins here, at the sealed road access off Namatjira Drive. The Ormiston Pound walk loops from the same car park through the gorge, and is worth a rest day if you have one to spare.

descriptions.name: R: Ormiston Gorge
descriptions.description: Food-drop point at Ormiston Gorge, the last one before the finish at Redbank Gorge. With a kiosk and a campground here as well, it is the easiest place on the trail to reset before the final sections.

descriptions.name: George Creek
descriptions.description: Creek camp just west of Ormiston Gorge on the short Section 10 walk out to the Finke. It is a bush site with no facilities, and any water in the creek bed is seasonal.

descriptions.name: Finke River
descriptions.description: Camp on the Finke, a broad sandy river bed and one of the oldest watercourses in the world. Water sits in scattered waterholes rather than a running stream, and the sand makes for slow walking wherever the trail follows the bed.

descriptions.name: Finke River Trailhead
descriptions.description: The boundary between Sections 10 and 11, where a vehicle track reaches the river. Access is rough, and the Glen Helen area out on Namatjira Drive is the nearest place with any services — check what is open before relying on it.

descriptions.name: Hill Top
descriptions.description: Ridge camp on Section 11 with a long view west to Mt Sonder. Up here it is exposed and dry with nothing to collect, so carry the night's water up from the Finke.

descriptions.name: Rocky Bar Gap
descriptions.description: Camp in a gap in the range on the last full section of the trail, sheltered between the ridgelines. It is a bush site with no facilities and no dependable water.

descriptions.name: Redbank
descriptions.description: Walkers' camp at Redbank Gorge, the end of the through-walk and the base for the Mt Sonder climb. Most people camp here the night before and set off in the dark to be on the summit at sunrise.

descriptions.name: Redbank Gorge
descriptions.description: Tank at the Redbank Gorge camping area, and the fill point for the Mt Sonder climb, which has nothing to drink on it at all. It is topped up by vehicle, so check it rather than assume, and take a full load up the hill.

descriptions.name: Redbank Gorge Trailhead
descriptions.description: Section 11 ends here and Section 12, the return climb of Mt Sonder, begins. The gorge itself is a narrow chasm holding a deep, cold waterhole, and Mt Sonder is a significant place to Arrernte people — walk it with that in mind and respect the signage.

descriptions.name: Ellery Creek North
descriptions.description: The Ellery Creek North camp as it is marked on the alternative high-route approach, which drops off the ridge to the creek rather than following the valley in. Facilities are basic and the tank is refilled by vehicle, so treat what you take and do not assume it is full.

descriptions.name: Counts Point
descriptions.description: High point on the Chewings ridgeline in Section 9 and the best viewpoint on the trail, with a long look west down the ranges towards Mt Sonder. It is exposed and waterless, so anyone stopping the night here has to carry everything up.
